title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Migraine is a prevalent primary headache disorder marked by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe pain, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia. Some patients experience an aura due to cortical spreading depression. The pathophysiology involves trigeminovascular activation, neurogenic inflammation, and cortical hyperexcitability. Standard management includes pharmacologic and behavioral therapies, yet a subset of patients develop chronic, drug-refractory migraine. For these individuals, advanced options such as botulinum toxin injections, peripheral nerve neurolysis or neurectomy, and neuromodulation with occipital nerve stimulation may be considered. Selection of appropriate surgical candidates requires careful clinical evaluation, recognition of trigger sites, and assessment of comorbidities to balance benefit with risks such as muscle weakness, neuropathic pain, or device-related complications.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This course strengthens clinicians' knowledge and competence in the evaluation and management of refractory migraine. Learners explore the mechanisms, techniques, and evidence supporting advanced interventions, and they develop strategies for safe patient selection and complication prevention. The curriculum highlights interprofessional collaboration among neurologists, surgeons, psychologists, psychiatrists, pharmacists, and specialty-trained nurses. Each professional brings unique expertise, encompassing medication optimization, behavioral health, surgical planning, and patient education. Collaborative care improves diagnostic accuracy, procedural safety, and adherence, ultimately enhancing patient outcomes and quality of life.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Assess the clinical features, severity scoring, and comorbidities of patients with refractory migraine to determine candidacy for advanced interventions in collaboration with an interprofessional healthcare team. Differentiate between pharmacologic, procedural, and neuromodulatory treatment options for migraine by interpreting available evidence and communicating effectively with other clinicians to guide shared decision-making. Implement evidence-based strategies for botulinum toxin injection, peripheral neurolysis, or neuromodulation while coordinating perioperative and postoperative care with nurses, pharmacists, and behavioral health specialists. Evaluate patient outcomes following advanced migraine therapies and improve long-term management plans through structured communication and collaboration across the interprofessional healthcare team. title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Introduction
content: Migraine is a primary neurologic disorder characterized by recurrent headache, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, or vertigo, and may present with or without aura. [1] The condition affects 11.7% of the United States population, including 17.1% of women and 5.6% of men. [2] Migraine can be episodic, acute, or chronic. Pharmacologic treatment includes β-blockers, anticonvulsants, calcium channel blockers, tricyclic antidepressants, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. [3] Migraine surgery is indicated when the condition is refractory to medical treatment. Chronic migraine is defined by the International Headache Society classification of headache disorders, third edition: Headache occurring ≥15 days/month. Duration > 3 months. Other features of migraine occurring ≥8 days/month.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Earlier theories proposed that migraine was generated by vasodilation of the cerebral vasculature; however, this mechanism has been refuted by several studies that showed an absence of migraine in response to vasoactive intestinal peptide, which increases blood flow. [4] Similarly, medications that precipitate migraine, like sildenafil, do not cause sustained vascular changes. [5] Furthermore, cortical and brainstem hyperexcitability may contribute to migraine pathophysiology, [6] [7] and cortical spreading depression is responsible for the aura. [8]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Trigeminal afferents project to the meninges and release pain mediators such as substance P, calcitonin gene–related peptide, and neurokinin A, leading to a cycle of neurogenic inflammation. [9] The strongest clinical evidence supports a peripheral origin of migraine, as demonstrated by the beneficial effect of botulinum toxin and peripheral neurolysis for chronic migraine. Migraine surgery focuses on neurolysis of sensory branches of the trigeminal and occipital nerves innervating the face and occiput. [10] These nerves include the supraorbital, supratrochlear, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal, and greater and lesser occipital nerves. Sometimes, the pain is also due to hypertrophic nasal turbinates or a deviated nasal septum that irritates branches of the trigeminal nerves.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Indications
content: Migraine surgery is indicated for a disease that is refractory to conservative measures, including medication and behavioral therapy.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Contraindications
content: The presence of a diagnosed psychiatric disorder is a relative contraindication to migraine surgery.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Personnel
content: All patients being considered for migraine surgery should first undergo evaluation by a neurologist.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Preparation
content: Migraine severity is assessed using several scales; the most widely used is the Migraine Disability Assessment questionnaire (MIDAS). [11] MIDAS grading is as follows: 0 to 5, grade I (little or no disability), 6 to 10, grade II (mild disability); 11 to 20, grade III (moderate disability); and greater than 21, grade IV (severe disability). The initial treatment of a migraine includes pharmacologic and behavioral therapies; however, the headaches can become refractory to these interventions. [12] [13]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Botulinum Toxin
content: The bacterium Clostridium botulinum produces botulinum toxin,  paralyzing muscles by inhibiting acetylcholine's release from presynaptic terminals. Botulinum toxin has 8 subtypes, A through H, of which type A is safe and effective for therapeutic use. [14] Justinus Kerner first used botulinum toxin as a medical therapeutic, which he called "sausage poison." He performed animal and human experiments, including on himself. [15] Alan Scott initially used botulinum toxin to treat strabismus. [14] Thereafter, the toxin was used in focal dystonias such as blepharospasm, [16] [17] cervical dystonia, [18] [19] oromandibular dystonia, [20] laryngeal dystonia, [21] hemifacial spasm, [20] [22] focal hand dystonia, [23] spasticity, focal hyperhidrosis, [24] and to diagnose and treat migraine trigger sites. [25]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Botulinum Toxin
content: Botulinum toxin reduces migraine frequency and severity by decreasing the irritation of the peripheral nerves by paralyzing the triggering muscles and decreasing the release of inflammatory mediators. [26] Results from several double-blind controlled trials demonstrated a 50% reduction in frequency and severity of migraines at 3 months, with efficacy lasting 3 to 4 months. [25] [27] [28] However, results from other studies reported only modest superiority of botulinum toxin over placebo. [29] [30] Although botulinum toxin can be used short-term as an acute and prophylactic treatment, [25] [27] long-term use is limited due to the development of resistance, diminished efficacy, and adverse effects such as muscle paralysis, atrophy, and irritation, especially with higher doses. [25] [31] Therefore, some experts recommend using it only as a screening tool before neurolysis. [32]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Botulinum Toxin
content: Botulinum toxin is injected into the pericranial muscles at multiple sites according to the location of the pain. The most commonly used safe and effective dose is 25 U in normal saline. This total dose can be divided into 3 U for each temporalis muscle (total, 6 U), 2.5 U at 4 frontalis muscle sites (5 U unilaterally; 10 U bilaterally), 3 U into each corrugator muscle (total, 6 U), and 3 U into the procerus muscle in the midline. [25] For occipital headaches, 12.5 to 50 U may be injected on each side of the midline near the greater and lesser occipital nerves. Pain relief lasting 6 to 12 weeks indicates that the patient is an appropriate surgical candidate.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Peripheral Neurolysis/Neurectomy
content: The beneficial effect of peripheral neurolysis of the supratrochlear and supraorbital nerves on migraine was first recognized when Guyuron found that his patients were relieved of a debilitating migraine after brow lift surgery. [33] Subsequently, the group published a prospective study confirming the findings. [34] Neurolysis is performed after identification of trigger sites and demonstration of greater than 50% pain relief for at least 6 weeks following botulinum toxin injection. Botulinum toxin is injected into the bilateral frontal, temporal, and occipital regions (12.5 U each) or the corrugator supercilii muscles. [34] [35] Evaluation for hypertrophied nasal turbinates irritating the trigeminal nerves of the nasal septum should also be performed. Peripheral neurectomy is also effective for treating drug-refractory migraine. [36]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Peripheral Neurolysis/Neurectomy
content: Frontal headache: An eyelid incision retracts the orbital septum caudally, and the orbicularis oculi is retracted cranially. The corrugator supercilii and depressor supercilii are resected, and the nerves are freed. Both supraorbital and supratrochlear blood vessels are ligated, and the supraorbital foramen is unroofed. The space is filled with the medial orbital fat and fixed with 6-0 polyglactin 910 sutures. The incisions are then closed with 6-0 nylon sutures. This procedure can be performed bilaterally. [34]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Peripheral Neurolysis/Neurectomy
content: Anterior temporal headache: The treatment of anterior temporal headache consists of severing the zygomaticotemporal nerve. For a frontotemporal headache, the procedure is combined with that for frontal headaches by making 2 incisions, one in the upper tarsal crease and another at the superior temporal line. [35] These procedures can also be performed endoscopically. [34] The zygomaticotemporal nerve is located 16 mm lateral and 6 mm cranial to the lateral canthus. A 2 cm incision is made at this point, and dissection is performed between the 2 layers of the temporalis fascia. The nerve is severed and located at the lateral margin of the orbit. The distal aspect is buried deep in the muscle, and closure is performed in layers.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Peripheral Neurolysis/Neurectomy
content: Posterior temporal headache: The auriculotemporal nerve is the most common cause of this type of headache. A 2 cm incision is made at the base of the zygomatic arch. The nerve and superficial temporal blood vessels are identified, and the blood vessels are ligated. The nerve is isolated for 1 to 2 cm, severed, and buried in the temporalis muscle. The incision is closed in layers.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Peripheral Neurolysis/Neurectomy
content: Occipital headache: In cases of occipital migraine, occipital nerve neurolysis from the semispinalis capitis muscle can be performed. [37] For diffuse occipital region pain, greater occipital neurolysis is performed. A midline incision is made from the external occipital protuberance to the C2 spinous process. The trapezius fascia is incised approximately 1 cm from the midline. The trapezius fibers are split in line, and dissection is performed below them to locate the greater occipital nerve. The semispinalis capitis muscle around the nerve is transected to free the nerve. Similarly, the trapezius muscle and fascia over the nerve are removed. The procedure can be repeated contralaterally. Pedicled fat is removed from the overlying skin, inserted between the nerve and muscle, and sutured. The incision is closed with 3-0 nylon sutures.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Peripheral Neurolysis/Neurectomy
content: For lateral occipital headache, lesser occipital neurolysis or neurectomy can be performed. A 2 cm incision is made about 2 cm medial to the mastoid in the hairline. The thick temporal fascia is incised. The lesser occipital nerve and blood vessel are dissected. The artery is coagulated and ligated. The nerve is dissected out for about 1 to 2 cm, severed, and buried in the muscle. The incision is closed with 3-0 nylon sutures. Occipital neurolysis offers immediate relief but also has a high rate of recurrence, [37] although alternative options such as neuromodulation are available.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Peripheral Neurolysis/Neurectomy
content: Rhinogenic headaches: If hypertrophied turbinates or a deviated nasal septum are identified as the cause of headache, turbinectomy or septoplasty is performed. The branches of the maxillary nerve through the sphenopalatine ganglion mediate this type of headache, and botulinum toxin treatment is ineffective.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Neuromodulation for Migraine
content: Neuromodulation is performed if patients do not experience relief with medical management or if peripheral neurolysis is not feasible or beneficial. The initial option is occipital nerve stimulation, which is achieved by placing electrodes around cervical dorsal nerves in the suboccipital region and connecting them first to a trial stimulator. If greater than 50% pain relief is achieved, the electrodes are connected to a permanently implantable pulse generator. Other options for neuromodulation include sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation, [38] supraorbital nerve stimulation, [39] [40] and vagus nerve stimulation. [41] [42] Although these interventions have demonstrated benefit in initial studies, large controlled trials are needed. [43] Occipital nerve stimulation modulates nociceptive transmission in the trigeminocervical complex, likely by activating large-diameter afferent fibers that inhibit pain signaling from small nociceptive fibers (gate control theory). [44]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Neuromodulation for Migraine
content: Occipital nerve stimulation provides analgesia in the distribution of both occipital and trigeminal nerves through modulation of the trigeminocervical complex when the trigeminal nucleus and portions of the upper 3 cervical dorsal nerves are stimulated. Approximately 30% to 50% of patients achieve greater than 50% pain relief. [45] [46] [47] This procedure has a high rate of lead readjustment (approximately 50%), but it is minimally invasive. [47] Occipital nerve stimulation has also demonstrated benefit in cluster headaches. [48]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Technique or Treatment -- Nerve Decompression
content: Decompression of nerves at the trigger site (frontal, temporal, occipital) by removing surrounding tissues, including muscles and blood vessels, can be helpful for patients with medically refractory, chronic migraine. [49]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Complications -- Botulinum Toxin
content: Patients may experience transient atrophy of injected muscles, especially the temporalis muscle. The incidence rate can be as high as 23%. [50] Other complications include transient eyelid ptosis when injections involve the frontalis muscle or neck muscle weakness when injections involve the cervical region.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Complications -- Peripheral Neurolysis/Neurectomy
content: Patients can have neuroma formation when neuromyotomy is performed, which can be prevented by burying the severed nerve end in the muscle. Infection and hemorrhage can occur, but the incidence is low. Temporary paresthesia and pruritus at the surgical site are also possible. [51]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Complications -- Turbinate Surgery
content: Postoperative complications include epistaxis, sinusitis, nasal dryness, or septal deviation. [50]

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Complications -- Neuromodulation
content: Lead migration can occur if not anchored properly. Infection is managed with antibiotics and rarely requires implant removal.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Clinical Significance
content: A migraine is a common primary headache disorder. A neurologist evaluates clinical features and the MIDAS score to assess severity. Initial treatment includes pharmacologic and behavioral therapies. Botulinum toxin is commonly used to identify the trigger sites. Peripheral neurolysis or neurectomy is an effective treatment for drug-refractory cases.

title: Migraine Surgical Interventions -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Patients with migraines should be evaluated by an interprofessional team that includes a neurologist, psychologist, psychiatrist, surgeon, specialty-trained neurology nurse, and other healthcare professionals. Appropriate case selection is necessary for a successful surgical outcome. A pharmacist should assist with pharmaceutical selection and monitoring. Nurses should provide preoperative and postoperative patient education to ensure optimal care.
